title: Packaged products: the pooled-vehicle family, pricing, and share classes

reading.body:
A **packaged product** pools money from many investors. It hands each one back a share of a professional portfolio. The exam wants you to tell the wrappers apart, because they price and trade in different ways.

Learn to spot five on sight. An **open-end fund** is a mutual fund. It issues new shares all the time, and the fund buys them back. A **closed-end fund** has a fixed number of shares that trade on an exchange like a stock. A **unit investment trust (UIT)** holds a fixed, unmanaged portfolio of redeemable units. An **exchange-traded fund (ETF)** holds a basket that tracks an index or a manager's picks, trades all day, and stays near NAV. The **exchange-traded note (ETN)** is the odd one out. It is not a fund at all.

reading.h: Open-end vs. closed-end — where the price comes from
reading.body:
An **open-end (mutual) fund** always trades in the primary market. You buy new shares from the fund at the **public offering price (POP)**. You redeem them back to the fund at **net asset value (NAV)**. You can never buy an open-end share below NAV.

A **closed-end fund** raises a fixed pool once, in an IPO. After that its shares trade **secondary** on an exchange, and supply and demand set the price. That price can be a **premium or a discount to NAV**, and most trade at a discount. So a fund quoted below its reported NAV is a closed-end fund, not a mutual fund. You buy closed-end shares with a **commission**. You can margin them and sell them short. The fund may also issue preferred stock and bonds, which is leverage.

**NAV per share = (total assets − liabilities) ÷ shares outstanding.** The fund computes it at least once a day, at the 4:00 p.m. ET close. Buying or selling fund shares does not move NAV per share, because assets and shares rise together. Paying a distribution lowers NAV by the amount paid.

**Forward pricing (Rule 22c-1)** fills every purchase and redemption at the next NAV after the order arrives. An order at 2:00 p.m. gets that day's 4:00 p.m. price. An order at 4:30 p.m. gets tomorrow's price. Filling an order after the close at today's known price is illegal **late trading**.

reading.h: Loads and the A / B / C share classes
reading.body:
A **load** is a sales charge. It is always a percent of the POP, never of NAV. So **POP = NAV ÷ (1 − sales charge %)**. A fund with a $9.50 NAV and a 5% load has a POP of 9.50 ÷ 0.95 = **$10.00**. It is not 9.50 × 1.05.

The same portfolio comes in three share classes. **Class A** takes a front-end load up front. It offers **breakpoints** and a low yearly 12b-1 fee, so it fits large amounts and long holding periods. **Class B** has no front load. It has a **back-end contingent deferred sales charge (CDSC)** that drops to zero over several years, plus a high 12b-1 fee. Class B **converts to Class A** in time. **Class C** charges a **level load** of about 1% every year, with little or no front or back charge. It has no breakpoints and no conversion. Class C is cheapest for a short holding period and worst for the long haul.

reading.h: Getting a discount: breakpoints, LOI, ROA
reading.body:
**Breakpoints** are quantity discounts on Class A. The more you invest, the lower the sales-charge percent, per a schedule in the prospectus. Recommending a purchase just below a breakpoint to earn a bigger charge is a prohibited **breakpoint sale**.

A **letter of intent (LOI)** is a non-binding pledge to invest enough within **13 months** to reach a breakpoint. Every purchase gets the discount, and the fund holds some shares in **escrow** in case you do not finish. You may backdate the LOI up to **90 days**. Only new money counts; appreciation and reinvested dividends do not.

**Rights of accumulation (ROA)** work once your holdings plus the new purchase cross a breakpoint. Value the holdings at the higher of current value or cost. The new money then gets the lower rate. There is no time limit and no refund on the old shares.

reading.h: ETFs and the impostor, the ETN
reading.body:
An **ETF** is usually an open-end fund or UIT that trades all day on an exchange. **Creation and redemption** keep its price near NAV. Authorized participants swap a basket of the underlying securities for large blocks of shares **in kind**. In-kind redemptions also make ETFs **tax-efficient**, because the fund does not sell and realize gains. Investors pay a commission and a bid-ask spread, not a sales load.

An **ETN** looks similar but is **unsecured debt of a bank**. It carries the **issuer's credit risk** and is not a fund at all. **Leveraged and inverse ETFs reset daily.** Over holds of more than a day, compounding pulls their return away from the stated multiple. FINRA treats them as generally **unsuitable for buy-and-hold retail investors**.

An **annuity** is an insurance contract. The exam's first question is who bears the investment risk. In a **fixed annuity** the premium goes into the insurer's **general account**. The insurer guarantees the rate and the payment, so the **insurer bears investment risk**. You bear purchasing-power (inflation) risk, and a fixed annuity is not a security. In a **variable annuity** the premium goes into a **separate account** invested in subaccounts. The **owner bears the investment risk**. Because it is a security, it needs a **prospectus** and a rep with both a securities and an insurance license. Module 30 goes deep. For now, lock in one line: fixed = insurer's risk, variable = owner's risk.

flashcards.front: Which pooled vehicle can trade BELOW its NAV?
flashcards.back: A closed-end fund. Its shares trade secondary, priced by supply and demand. Open-end shares always sell at POP and redeem at NAV.
(Total assets − liabilities) ÷ shares outstanding, computed at the 4:00 p.m. ET close.
Every purchase or redemption fills at the next NAV after the order arrives. A 2 p.m. order gets the 4 p.m. price.
POP = NAV ÷ (1 − sales charge %). The sales charge is a percent of POP, never of NAV.

flashcards.front: Class A vs. B vs. C — best use
flashcards.back: A: large amounts, long term (breakpoints, front load). B: back-end CDSC that drops, converts to A. C: short term (level load, no breakpoints, no conversion).

flashcards.front: LOI vs. ROA — the two differences
flashcards.back: LOI: 13-month forward pledge, backdate up to 90 days, escrow, new money only (no appreciation). ROA: no time limit, counts current value, no refund on old shares.

flashcards.front: What keeps an ETF near NAV?
flashcards.back: Creation and redemption of shares in kind by authorized participants. This also makes ETFs tax-efficient.
Unsecured debt of a bank. It carries issuer credit risk. It is not a fund.
They reset daily. Over holds of more than a day, compounding pulls the return away from the stated multiple. Generally unsuitable for buy-and-hold retail.

flashcards.front: Fixed vs. variable annuity — who bears investment risk?
flashcards.back: Fixed: insurer (general account). Variable: owner (separate account, a security).
Illegally entering an order after the 4 p.m. close at today's known price. Forward pricing forbids it.
Recommending a purchase just below a breakpoint so the rep earns a higher sales charge.

quiz.stem: A customer sees shares of an investment company quoted at $18.40 while the fund reports a net asset value of $20.00 per share. This fund is MOST likely:
options: A closed-end fund whose shares trade on an exchange at a discount to NAV
An open-end fund selling below NAV to attract new investors
A no-load open-end fund
A money market fund that has broken the buck
quiz.explanation: Open-end shares are always sold at POP and redeemed at NAV, never below NAV, so a price under reported NAV must be a closed-end fund, whose exchange price is set by supply and demand and can sit at a discount. A no-load open-end fund still transacts at NAV, not below it.

quiz.stem: A customer places an order to buy shares of a mutual fund at 2:00 p.m. ET. Under forward pricing, the price the customer pays is based on:
options: The NAV computed at that day's 4:00 p.m. close
The NAV from the prior day's close
The NAV at the moment the order was entered, 2:00 p.m.
The average NAV for the week
quiz.explanation: Rule 22c-1 forward pricing fills the order at the NEXT NAV computed after receipt — here that day's 4:00 p.m. calculation. Using a price already known at 2:00 p.m. or the prior close would be the mispricing the rule exists to prevent (that is late trading).

quiz.stem: An open-end fund has a net asset value of $9.50 per share and a 5% sales charge. Its public offering price is:
quiz.explanation: The sales charge is a percentage of POP, so POP = NAV ÷ (1 − 0.05) = 9.50 ÷ 0.95 = $10.00. The trap is 9.50 × 1.05 = $9.975, which treats the load as a percentage of NAV.

quiz.stem: An investor plans to invest a large lump sum and hold it for 20 years. Which mutual fund share class is generally MOST appropriate?
options: Class A, because breakpoints reduce the sales charge and the ongoing 12b-1 fee is low
Class B, because the back-end charge is waived after one year
Class C, because the level load is cheapest for a long holding period
It makes no difference; all classes cost the same over time
quiz.explanation: A large amount qualifies for Class A breakpoints, and A's low 12b-1 fee compounds cheaply over a long horizon. Class C's ~1% annual level load is worst over 20 years, and Class B's CDSC plus high 12b-1 also costs more than A's discounted front load for a large, long-term investment.

quiz.stem: An exchange-traded note (ETN) differs from an ETF in that an ETN is:
options: A basket of stocks redeemable in kind by authorized participants
An unsecured debt obligation of the issuing bank, carrying issuer credit risk
A closed-end fund that trades at a discount to NAV
Guaranteed by the FDIC up to $250,000
quiz.explanation: An ETN is unsecured debt of a bank, so its value depends on the issuer's creditworthiness — it is not a fund and holds no basket of securities. The in-kind creation/redemption description applies to ETFs, and ETNs carry no FDIC insurance.

quiz.stem: During the accumulation period of a variable annuity, the investment risk is borne by:
options: The insurance company, which guarantees a minimum rate of return
The contract owner, whose premiums are invested in a separate account
The broker-dealer that sold the contract
The state insurance guaranty association
quiz.explanation: Variable annuity premiums go into a separate account whose value fluctuates, so the owner bears investment risk. In a FIXED annuity the insurer's general account bears investment risk and the owner instead bears purchasing-power (inflation) risk.

quiz.stem: A customer signs a letter of intent (LOI) to reach a $50,000 breakpoint. Which statement is TRUE?
options: The LOI is binding, and failing to complete it results in a FINRA fine
The customer has 13 months to complete the purchases, and the LOI may be backdated up to 90 days to capture a prior purchase
Appreciation on shares already owned counts toward completing the LOI
All purchases must be completed within 90 days of signing
quiz.explanation: An LOI is a non-binding pledge to invest enough within 13 months, and it may be backdated up to 90 days to include an earlier purchase. Only new money counts — appreciation and reinvested dividends do not — and non-completion simply triggers the higher charge via escrowed shares, not a fine.

quiz.stem: All of the following are characteristics of a unit investment trust (UIT) EXCEPT:
options: It has no board of directors
Its portfolio is fixed rather than actively traded
Units are redeemable through the sponsor
It employs an investment adviser who actively manages the portfolio for an ongoing fee
quiz.explanation: A UIT is organized under a trust indenture with a fixed, unmanaged portfolio, redeemable units, and NO board of directors and NO investment adviser — so there is no ongoing management fee. The other three are all defining UIT traits.
